planting.note: Grow in a hanging basket or on a small trellis in bright, indirect light with a chunky, fast-draining epiphyte mix; this Himalayan species prefers cooler nights and slightly more airflow than lowland hoyas.

directions: Hoya polyneura is a cool-growing Himalayan epiphyte prized for its narrow, ribbed leaves whose pale veining resembles a fish skeleton on slender, cascading stems. It produces small, reflexed, cream-to-pink pinwheel flowers in loose pendant clusters and appreciates brighter, cooler conditions than many tropical hoyas, along with a distinct dip in watering through winter. Mount or basket it so the trailing stems hang freely, and avoid the deep shade and constant warmth suited to lowland species. Leave old flower spurs intact, since they rebloom repeatedly once the vine matures.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Train onto a sturdy trellis or moss pole in bright, indirect light; give this large-flowered Bornean species ample root room and a chunky, fast-draining mix, as it grows into a substantial vine.

directions: Native to Borneo's lowland forests, Hoya imperialis is a vigorous, large-leaved climber that produces some of the biggest flowers in the genus, with clusters of deep maroon-red, star-shaped blooms up to three inches across held on stout, woody spurs. It wants warmth, high humidity, and bright but filtered light to flower well, and its heavy stems benefit from a substantial trellis or arch rather than a small hanging basket. Let the coarse, chunky mix dry slightly between waterings and feed regularly during active growth to support its large leaves and flower trusses. Never cut back the woody spurs, since repeat blooms emerge from the same points for years.

common_name: Fragrant Star Hoya (Waxy Star Wax Plant)

planting.note: Grow in a hanging basket or on a small trellis in bright, indirect light with a very well-drained, chunky mix; this Southeast Asian species is prone to rot if kept wet.

directions: Hoya coronaria bears thick, succulent, deeply veined leaves on a compact twining vine and produces unusually large, fuzzy-textured, waxy star flowers that range from cream to deep maroon and release a strong, sweet fragrance after dusk. Its succulent leaves store water, so the coarse, fast-draining mix should dry well between waterings to avoid stem and root rot. Provide a small trellis or allow it to trail from a basket in bright, filtered light, and keep it warm and humid during active growth for the best flowering. Leave spent flower spurs in place, as they produce repeat blooms over successive seasons.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Grow in a hanging basket or on a small trellis in bright, indirect light with a chunky, fast-draining mix; this fast-growing Philippine species is one of the quickest hoyas to reach blooming size.

directions: Hoya bilobata is a compact, fast-growing Philippine species with small, glossy, deep green leaves on wiry twining stems, producing clusters of small red to maroon star-shaped flowers with a pale yellow corona that appear readily even on young plants. Its quick growth and free-flowering habit make it a good choice for beginners wanting an early hoya bloom, and it tolerates lower light than many species while still flowering. Keep the chunky, well-drained mix evenly moist but never soggy, and provide a small trellis or twine for the twining stems to climb. Leave the woody flower spurs in place once they form, since they rebloom repeatedly.

planting.note: Grow in a hanging basket in bright, indirect light with a fast-draining, chunky mix; this Indian species has thin, grass-like leaves and tolerates brighter light and drier conditions than most hoyas.

directions: Hoya retusa is an unusual Indian species with narrow, stiff, grass-like leaves borne densely along thin, wiry, pendant stems, giving mature plants an almost tufted, fountain-like appearance quite unlike the broad-leaved hoyas. It produces small clusters of white, star-shaped flowers with a red-tipped corona and tolerates brighter light and drier soil than most species in the genus, making it well suited to a sunny windowsill or bright shelf. Let the fast-draining mix dry out between waterings, and mount or basket the plant so its stiff leaves and trailing habit can be appreciated. Once flower spurs form, leave them undisturbed for repeat bloom.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Train onto a substantial trellis or arch in bright, indirect light; this large-leaved Indonesian species needs ample room and a chunky, fast-draining mix as it matures into a big specimen vine.

directions: Hoya coriacea is a robust Indonesian climber with long, drooping, leathery leaves that can reach a foot or more in length, giving mature specimens a dramatic, curtain-like presence on a large trellis or arch. Its pendant clusters of cream to pale yellow, waxy flowers open with a strong, sweet evening fragrance and are produced from the same woody spurs year after year. Give it generous space, bright filtered light, and a coarse, well-drained mix that is allowed to dry slightly between thorough waterings. Feed regularly through the growing season to support its large leaves and vigorous climbing growth.
